q: Atoms of elements are rarely found by themselves in nature.
e: True. Atoms of elements are rarely found by themselves in nature. They are almost always joined as molecules or as compounds.

q: The attractive forces that hold atoms together in compounds are also known as intermolecular forces.
e: False. Atoms inside a compound are held by chemical bonds. Intermolecular forces only tug neighbouring molecules toward each other.

q: The outermost shell electrons of atoms are the basis for understanding the joining of atoms.
e: True. The outermost shell electrons of atoms are the basis for understanding the joining of atoms. Those outer electrons, the valence electrons, are the ones that actually form bonds.

q: According to the Aufbau principle, electrons are filled in the higher energy atomic orbitals before filling lower energy ones.
e: False. Aufbau fills lower-energy orbitals first. Higher-energy orbitals wait until the lower ones are already occupied.

q: The order of filling the orbitals is given as 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p.
e: True. The order of filling the orbitals is given as 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p. 4s fills before 3d, which is why that order looks out of numerical sequence.

q: Pauli's exclusion principle states that no more than three electrons can occupy the same orbital.
e: False. Pauli's rule allows only two electrons in one orbital. Those two must also have opposite spins.

q: Two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins.
e: True. Two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins. That opposite-spin pairing is Pauli's exclusion principle.

q: Hund's rule states that every orbital in a subshell is doubly occupied before any one orbital is singly occupied.
e: False. Hund puts one electron in each orbital of a subshell before any pairing. You do not fill one orbital with two electrons first.

q: The s subshell has only one spherical-shaped orbital.
e: True. The s subshell has only one spherical-shaped orbital. That one s orbital holds two electrons.

q: There are five dumbbell-shaped p orbitals in an atom.
e: False. There are three p orbitals, px, py and pz, and each is dumbbell-shaped. Five orbitals of that kind would be the d set, not p.

q: Each p subshell can be filled with a maximum of 10 electrons.
e: False. A p subshell holds six electrons, two in each of three orbitals. Ten electrons is the capacity of a d subshell.

q: For an atom, the number of valence electrons is equal to its group number in the Periodic Table.
e: True. For an atom, the number of valence electrons is equal to its group number in the Periodic Table. That match is for main-group atoms, where the group number counts the outer electrons.

q: Whenever a chemical bond forms, atoms lose, gain, or share electrons in order to achieve the stable electronic structures of noble gases.
e: True. Whenever a chemical bond forms, atoms lose, gain, or share electrons in order to achieve the stable electronic structures of noble gases. That drive is the octet rule, or a duplet for hydrogen and helium.

q: The octet rule strictly applies to all d-block elements without exceptions.
e: False. The octet rule is a main-group guide. d-block metals often keep extra d electrons or expand beyond eight.

q: Electronegativity is a measure of the ability of an atom to attract the shared electrons to itself.
e: True. Electronegativity is a measure of the ability of an atom to attract the shared electrons to itself. A larger electronegativity means a stronger pull on the shared pair.

q: Electron affinity is the amount of energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom.
e: False. Energy to remove an electron is ionisation energy. Electron affinity is the energy released when a gaseous atom gains an electron.

q: Elements having high electron affinity easily gain electrons, resulting in the formation of anions.
e: True. Elements having high electron affinity easily gain electrons, resulting in the formation of anions. Gaining electrons makes anions.

q: Generally, the higher the first ionisation energy of an element, the lower is its electronegativity.
e: False. A high first ionisation energy usually goes with high electronegativity. Both mean the atom holds its electrons tightly.

q: The three main types of chemical bonding are ionic bonding, covalent bonding, and hydrogen bonding.
e: False. The three main intramolecular types are ionic, covalent, and metallic. Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular force.

q: In general, an ionic bond is stronger than a covalent bond.
e: True. In general, an ionic bond is stronger than a covalent bond. The full-charge electrostatic pull is usually stronger than a shared pair.

q: The hydrogen bond is the strongest intermolecular force followed by van der Waals forces.
e: True. The hydrogen bond is the strongest intermolecular force followed by van der Waals forces. Van der Waals forces, including London forces, come after hydrogen bonding in strength.

q: Among van der Waals forces, dipole-dipole interactions are the weakest intermolecular forces that can be found in all substances.
e: False. London dispersion forces are the weakest van der Waals attractions, and they appear in every substance. Dipole-dipole forces need polar molecules.

q: Most bonds are 100% ionic or 100% covalent.
e: False. Most real bonds have a mix of ionic and covalent character. A 100% pure type is the exception, not the rule.

q: In atoms, there are K, L, M, N main shells and each main shell can be divided into s, p, d, and f subshells.
e: True. In atoms, there are K, L, M, N main shells and each main shell can be divided into s, p, d, and f subshells. S, p, d, and f are the subshells inside those main shells.

q: Only core electrons can take part in chemical bonding.
e: False. Only valence electrons take part in bonding. Core electrons stay in inner shells.

q: Ionic bonding results from the transfer of electrons from one atom having small ionisation energy to another atom having a large electron affinity.
e: True. Ionic bonding results from the transfer of electrons from one atom having small ionisation energy to another atom having a large electron affinity. The metal loses electrons and the non-metal gains them.

q: Ionic bonding mostly takes place when the difference in electronegativity between two atoms is less than 1.8.
e: False. Ionic bonding is likely when the electronegativity difference is greater than about 1.8. A small difference points to covalent sharing.

q: Ionic bonding generally occurs between reactive metals and reactive non-metals.
e: True. Ionic bonding generally occurs between reactive metals and reactive non-metals. A large electronegativity gap is what lets the electrons transfer.

q: When an ionic bond forms, a metal gains electrons to form negatively charged ions.
e: False. The metal loses electrons and becomes a cation. The non-metal is the one that gains electrons and becomes an anion.

q: The number of lost or gained electrons by an atom during ionic bonding is the same as the valency of that element.
e: True. The number of lost or gained electrons by an atom during ionic bonding is the same as the valency of that element. Valency here is simply how many electrons were lost or gained.

q: In the formation of sodium chloride, the difference in electronegativity between Na and Cl is 2.1.
e: True.  In the formation of sodium chloride, the difference in electronegativity between Na and Cl is 2. 1.  That gap is greater than 1.

q: Both $Na^+$ and $Cl^-$ ions have the electronic configurations of the noble gases Ne and Ar, respectively.
e: True. Both Na+ and Cl- ions have the electronic configurations of the noble gases Ne and Ar, respectively. Na+ is isoelectronic with neon and Cl- with argon.

q: In ionic compounds, the greater the charge on the ions, the weaker the electrostatic attraction.
e: False. Higher ionic charges pull more strongly. That stronger lattice attraction is why MgO melts higher than NaCl.

q: The melting points of the ionic compounds with the greater charge on the ions are higher.
e: True. The melting points of the ionic compounds with the greater charge on the ions are higher. Higher charge means a stronger lattice pull, so more heat is needed to melt the solid.

q: In solid ionic compounds, ions can move freely and hence they can conduct electricity.
e: False. In the solid the ions are locked in the lattice, so they cannot carry a current. They conduct when molten or dissolved, when they can move.

q: The crystalline structure of an ionic solid is called a crystal lattice.
e: True. The crystalline structure of an ionic solid is called a crystal lattice. Ions occupy a repeating 3D pattern, not random positions.

q: The cubic unit cell can have three types: simple cubic, face-centred cubic, and body-centred cubic.
e: True. The cubic unit cell can have three types: simple cubic, face-centred cubic, and body-centred cubic. Those three differ by whether extra atoms sit on faces or in the cube centre.

q: Sodium chloride has a simple cubic unit cell structure.
e: False. Sodium chloride has a face-centred cubic lattice. Each ion sits in an octahedral hole of the other kind, not a simple cubic cell.

q: In a sodium chloride crystal lattice, each $Na^+$ ion has eight neighbouring $Cl^-$ ions.
e: False. Each Na+ is surrounded by six Cl- ions, and each Cl- by six Na+. The coordination is 6:6, not 8.

q: The term coordination number is used to express the number of ions surrounding the central ion in the lattice.
e: True. The term coordination number is used to express the number of ions surrounding the central ion in the lattice. In NaCl that number is 6 around each ion.

q: Since the coordination ratio of $Na^+$ ion to $Cl^-$ ion is 6:6, the simple ratio of 1:1 gives the formula unit of sodium chloride which is NaCl.
e: True. Since the coordination ratio of Na+ ion to Cl- ion is 6:6, the simple ratio of 1:1 gives the formula unit of sodium chloride which is NaCl. 6:6 reduces to 1:1, which is why the formula is NaCl.

q: Electrostatic attraction is the attraction between a negatively charged ion and a positively charged ion.
e: True. Electrostatic attraction is the attraction between a negatively charged ion and a positively charged ion. That +/− pull is the ionic bond.

q: A unit cell is the largest repeating unit of a crystal lattice that shows the three-dimensional pattern.
e: False. The unit cell is the smallest repeating block. Stack that small cell and you rebuild the whole crystal.

q: In the case of magnesium oxide, Mg loses two electrons, and oxygen gains two electrons to result in $Mg^{2+}$ and $O^{2-}$ ions.
e: True. In the case of magnesium oxide, Mg loses two electrons, and oxygen gains two electrons to result in Mg2+ and O2- ions. The charges become 2+ and 2-, so the formula is MgO.

q: Ionic compounds are always electrically charged due to the transfer of electrons.
e: False. The whole ionic compound is electrically neutral. Cations and anions are present in a ratio that cancels charge.

q: Covalent bonding can occur between similar or even identical atoms.
e: True. Covalent bonding can occur between similar or even identical atoms. Two non-metals, even two identical atoms, can share a pair.

q: A covalent bond is formed by transferring one or more pairs of valence electrons between atoms.
e: False. Transferring electrons makes an ionic bond. A covalent bond is a shared pair, not a transfer.

q: The covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of the atoms and the shared electrons.
e: True. The covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of the atoms and the shared electrons. The two nuclei both pull the shared pair, and that pull is the covalent bond.

q: Covalent bonding usually occurs between metals.
e: False. Covalent bonding is typical between non-metals. Metals more often form metallic or ionic bonding.

q: When two hydrogen atoms are too close to each other, the attractive interaction between two nuclei becomes so strong that it pushes them apart.
e: False. If the nuclei get too close, repulsion between the two positive nuclei pushes them apart. Attraction is not what drives them away at that tiny distance.

q: The bond length is the optimum distance between two nuclei where net attractive forces are maximised.
e: True. The bond length is the optimum distance between two nuclei where net attractive forces are maximised. Closer than that, nuclear repulsion wins; further away, the shared-pair attraction weakens.

q: In covalent bonding, the paired valence electrons are the ones primarily involved in overlapping and bonding.
e: False. Unpaired valence electrons in half-filled orbitals are the ones that overlap to make the covalent pair. Already-paired lone pairs do not usually do that job.

q: By overlapping orbitals, the outer shells of all the bonding atoms are filled with valence electrons by following the octet rule.
e: True. By overlapping orbitals, the outer shells of all the bonding atoms are filled with valence electrons by following the octet rule. Unpaired outer electrons pair up in the overlap region.

q: A double bond is formed by sharing three pairs of electrons between two atoms.
e: False. A double bond is two shared pairs. Three shared pairs make a triple bond.

q: The length of the bond is determined by the number of bonded electrons.
e: True. The length of the bond is determined by the number of bonded electrons. More shared pairs pull the atoms closer, so triple bonds are shortest.

q: The higher the number of bonded electrons, the longer the bond length.
e: False. More shared pairs pull the nuclei closer, so a triple bond is shorter than a double, which is shorter than a single. Bond length falls as bond order rises.

q: The bond strength of the triple bond is the highest, followed by the double bond and single bond.
e: True. The bond strength of the triple bond is the highest, followed by the double bond and single bond. A single bond is weakest, a double is in the middle, a triple is strongest.

q: A coordinate bond is characterised by the fact that the two shared electrons are both donated by one of the participating atoms.
e: True. A coordinate bond is characterised by the fact that the two shared electrons are both donated by one of the participating atoms. That is a coordinate, or dative, bond.

q: A coordinate bond is formed when one of the participating atoms possesses a bonding pair of electrons.
e: False. A coordinate bond needs a lone pair on the donor atom. A bonding pair is already shared and is not the pair being donated.

q: A coordinate bond is expressed as an arrow, $ightarrow$, which indicates the direction in which the electrons are donated.
e: True. A coordinate bond is expressed as an arrow, ightarrow, which indicates the direction in which the electrons are donated. The arrow points from the donor atom toward the acceptor.

q: The ammonia molecule possesses a lone pair of electrons on the hydrogen atom.
e: False. The lone pair in ammonia sits on nitrogen. Each hydrogen has only the shared pair of its N-H bond.

q: The combination of ammonia and a hydrogen ion produces the positively charged ammonium ion, $NH_4^+$.
e: True. The combination of ammonia and a hydrogen ion produces the positively charged ammonium ion, NH4+. Nitrogen donates its lone pair to H+, making NH4+.

q: Molecules with incomplete octets are called electron-deficient molecules.
e: True. Molecules with incomplete octets are called electron-deficient molecules. BF3 is the usual example, with only six electrons around boron.

q: $BF_3$ can accept an electron pair from a molecule bearing a lone pair to form a coordinate compound.
e: True. BF3 can accept an electron pair from a molecule bearing a lone pair to form a coordinate compound. That acceptance makes a coordinate compound.

q: In carbon monoxide, the CO molecule has a triple bond that consists of three ordinary covalent bonds.
e: False. CO is triple-bonded, but one of those links is a coordinate bond from oxygen to carbon. It is not three ordinary covalent shares from one electron each.

q: Lewis structures are three-dimensional representations of how the valence shell electrons are arranged.
e: False. Lewis structures are two-dimensional electron-dot pictures. Shape in 3D is a VSEPR job, not a Lewis-diagram job.

q: When drawing Lewis structures for ions, it is necessary to add electrons to account for positive charges.
e: False. For a cation you subtract electrons, because the ion has already lost them. You add electrons only when you draw an anion.

q: In the $PF_5$ molecule, there are five single bonds present.
e: True. In the PF5 molecule, there are five single bonds present. Phosphorus has an expanded shell with ten electrons.

q: The central atom in an expanded valence shell molecule has valence electrons of less than 8.
e: False. An expanded valence shell means more than eight electrons on the central atom. Fewer than eight is electron-deficient, the opposite idea.

q: $BeCl_2$ and $SF_6$ are both examples of electron-deficient molecules.
e: False. BeCl2 is electron-deficient, but SF6 is expanded-octet, with twelve electrons on sulphur. Those two examples are not the same class.

q: The VSEPR theory is based on the idea that the three-dimensional geometry of a molecule is mostly determined by the attractive interactions of the electron pairs.
e: False. VSEPR is about repulsion. Electron pairs push apart, and the shape is the arrangement that keeps that repulsion smallest.

q: The electron pairs will arrange themselves to minimise repulsion effects from one another.
e: True. The electron pairs will arrange themselves to minimise repulsion effects from one another. That is the heart of VSEPR: electron pairs get as far apart as they can.

q: The repulsive interaction of electron pairs increases in the order of bonding pair-bonding pair < lone pair-bonding pair < lone pair-lone pair.
e: True. The repulsive interaction of electron pairs increases in the order of bonding pair-bonding pair < lone pair-bonding pair < lone pair-lone pair. Lone pairs take more space than bonding pairs, so they push harder.

q: Lone pairs of electrons in a molecule occupy less space compared with the bonding pairs of electrons.
e: False. Lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs. That extra push is why water is bent more tightly than the tetrahedral angle.

q: All diatomic molecules represent two points in space and are joined by a straight line, meaning they are linear.
e: True. All diatomic molecules represent two points in space and are joined by a straight line, meaning they are linear. Two atoms can only lie on a straight line, so every diatomic molecule is linear.

q: In the $CO_2$ molecule, the four bonding pairs are considered as four single units, giving it a tetrahedral shape.
e: False. Each C=O double bond counts as one electron region, so CO2 has two regions and is linear. It is not tetrahedral.

q: A molecule of type $AX_3$ without lone pairs has a triangular planar shape.
e: True. A molecule of type AX3 without lone pairs has a triangular planar shape. Three bonding regions and no lone pairs sit 120 degrees apart.

q: The bond angle of F-B-F in $BF_3$ is 109.5°.
e: False. BF3 is trigonal planar, so F-B-F is 120°. 109.5° is the tetrahedral angle.

q: In $NH_3$, the geometry of the electron pairs is tetrahedral, but the shape of the molecule is trigonal pyramidal.
e: True. In NH3, the geometry of the electron pairs is tetrahedral, but the shape of the molecule is trigonal pyramidal. Four electron pairs are tetrahedral, but you only see three atoms, so the shape is a pyramid.

q: The bond angle of H-N-H in $NH_3$ will be greater than 109.5°.
e: False. The lone pair on nitrogen squeezes the H-N-H angle below 109.5°. Ammonia is about 107°, not larger than tetrahedral.

q: A molecule of type $AX_2E_2$, such as $H_2O$, has a bent or V-shaped molecular shape.
e: True. A molecule of type AX2E2, such as H2O, has a bent or V-shaped molecular shape. Two bonding pairs and two lone pairs on oxygen make water V-shaped.

q: In a diamond, each carbon atom is joined to three other carbon atoms by strong covalent bonds.
e: False. In diamond each carbon is bonded to four others in a tetrahedral giant lattice. Three neighbours each is the graphite pattern.

q: There are no free electrons in a diamond giant structure.
e: True. There are no free electrons in a diamond giant structure. Every valence electron is locked in a C-C bond, so diamond does not conduct.

q: Graphite has a layer and planar structure formed by joining each carbon atom to the other three carbon atoms by covalent bonds.
e: True. Graphite has a layer and planar structure formed by joining each carbon atom to the other three carbon atoms by covalent bonds. Each carbon in a sheet has three covalent neighbours, and spare electrons are delocalised in the sheet.

q: There are strong covalent bonds between the flat layers of graphite.
e: False. Inside a graphite sheet the C-C bonds are strong, but the sheets are held only by weak London forces. That is why graphite shears and feels slippery.

q: Graphite can conduct electricity because it has free-moving electrons in each layer.
e: True. Graphite can conduct electricity because it has free-moving electrons in each layer. Those delocalised electrons in each layer can move when a voltage is applied.

q: Fullerene ($C_{60}$) and carbon nanotubes exist as giant covalent structures.
e: False. C60 and nanotubes are molecular forms of carbon, not infinite giant lattices like diamond. Each molecule has a finite cage or tube.

q: In quartz ($SiO_2$), each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, but each oxygen atom is bonded to only two silicon atoms.
e: True. In quartz (SiO2), each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, but each oxygen atom is bonded to only two silicon atoms. Quartz is a giant covalent lattice, not a small SiO2 molecule pile.

q: Silicon(IV) oxide conducts electricity easily because it has free moving electrons.
e: False. Quartz has no delocalised electrons. Every valence electron is locked in Si-O covalent bonds, so it is an insulator.

q: Intermolecular forces are responsible for most of the physical and chemical properties of matter.
e: True. Intermolecular forces are responsible for most of the physical and chemical properties of matter. Boiling point, melting point, and solubility come from those between-molecule pulls.

q: If the atoms in a covalent bond are not identical, the electrons will be equally shared.
e: False. Different atoms have different electronegativities, so the pair sits closer to the more electronegative atom. That bond is polar covalent.

q: A dipole moment of the molecule can be expressed numerically by taking into account the magnitude of the charge and the distance separating the charges.
e: True. A dipole moment of the molecule can be expressed numerically by taking into account the magnitude of the charge and the distance separating the charges. Charge times distance gives the size of the dipole.

q: If two different non-metal atoms are bonded, the atom with the higher electronegativity will attract the shared electron pair more strongly.
e: True. If two different non-metal atoms are bonded, the atom with the higher electronegativity will attract the shared electron pair more strongly. That uneven share is a polar covalent bond.

q: The covalent bond formed in HCl is non-polar.
e: False. Chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen, so HCl is polar. The shared pair leans toward Cl.

q: The H-F bond is more polar than H-Cl, H-Br, and H-I bonds.
e: True. The H-F bond is more polar than H-Cl, H-Br, and H-I bonds. Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so H-F has the largest halogen-hydride dipole.

q: In a covalent bond formed between two similar non-metal atoms, the shared electron pair is unequally attracted to the two atoms.
e: False. Two identical non-metal atoms pull the pair equally. That bond is non-polar covalent.

q: Any non-polar covalent bond has a zero dipole moment.
e: True. Any non-polar covalent bond has a zero dipole moment. Equal sharing means no plus end and no minus end.

q: All diatomic molecules containing polar covalent bonds are non-polar molecules.
e: False. A diatomic molecule with a polar bond, such as HCl, is a polar molecule. There is no second bond to cancel the dipole.

q: The $H_2O$ molecule has a bent shape and is a polar molecule.
e: True. The H2O molecule has a bent shape and is a polar molecule. The two O-H dipoles do not cancel, so water has a net dipole.

q: In the $CO_2$ molecule, the two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel the effect of each other, making it a polar molecule.
e: False. Those opposite dipoles do cancel, so CO2 is non-polar. Cancellation makes the molecule non-polar, not polar.

q: Van der Waals forces are strong forces which include dipole-dipole interaction, ion-dipole interaction, and hydrogen bonding.
e: False. van der Waals forces are weak intermolecular attractions. Hydrogen bonding is stronger than ordinary van der Waals forces and is usually named separately.

q: Dipole-dipole interactions are formed when two dipolar molecules interact with each other in space.
e: True. Dipole-dipole interactions are formed when two dipolar molecules interact with each other in space. The plus end of one lines up with the minus end of the other.

q: Ion-dipole interaction happens especially in solutions where a negative ion will be attracted to the positive pole of the polar molecule.
e: True. Ion-dipole interaction happens especially in solutions where a negative ion will be attracted to the positive pole of the polar molecule. That is why ionic solids dissolve in water: ions stick to the polar ends of H2O.

q: London dispersion forces are the strongest intermolecular forces that can be formed between atoms.
e: False. London forces are the weakest intermolecular attractions. Hydrogen bonding is much stronger.

q: An atom can develop a temporary dipole when the electrons are distributed unsymmetrically about the nucleus.
e: True. An atom can develop a temporary dipole when the electrons are distributed unsymmetrically about the nucleus. That fleeting dipole is the start of a London force.

q: London dispersion forces are also called induced dipole-induced dipole interactions.
e: True. London dispersion forces are also called induced dipole-induced dipole interactions. A temporary dipole on one atom induces a dipole on its neighbour.

q: London dispersion forces can only occur between polar molecules.
e: False. London forces act in every substance, including non-polar atoms and molecules. They come from temporary dipoles, not permanent ones.

q: Due to London dispersion forces, non-polar substances can condense into liquids and freeze into solids when the temperature is lowered sufficiently.
e: True. Due to London dispersion forces, non-polar substances can condense into liquids and freeze into solids when the temperature is lowered sufficiently. London forces, though weak, can still hold molecules in a liquid or solid when it is cold enough.

q: The formation of hydrogen bonds requires the first molecule to have hydrogen attached to a low electronegative atom.
e: False. Hydrogen bonding needs H attached to a highly electronegative atom, N, O, or F. A low-electronegativity neighbour cannot make that strong dipole.

q: Hydrogen bonding can occur as both intermolecular and intramolecular forces.
e: True. Hydrogen bonding can occur as both intermolecular and intramolecular forces. Intermolecular H-bonds sit between molecules; intramolecular ones sit inside one molecule.

q: A hydrogen bond is a special type of dipole-dipole interaction that is weaker than van der Waals forces.
e: False. Hydrogen bonds are stronger than ordinary van der Waals attractions. That extra strength is why ice floats and why alcohols have high boiling points.

q: The hydrogen bond is stronger than a covalent bond.
e: False. A hydrogen bond is still an intermolecular force, much weaker than a covalent bond. It is only the strongest among the intermolecular set.

q: Most of the metals are gases at room temperature.
e: False. Almost all metals are solids at room temperature. Mercury is the unusual liquid metal, not a gas.

q: In a metallic bond, the atoms share electrons to bond together just like in covalent bonds.
e: False. Metallic bonding is a lattice of cations in a delocalised sea of electrons. It is not a shared pair between two atoms like a covalent bond.

q: In a metallic bond, the valence electrons of the atoms are very loosely held, forming a common electron cloud.
e: True. In a metallic bond, the valence electrons of the atoms are very loosely held, forming a common electron cloud. That cloud is the metallic sea of delocalised valence electrons.

q: These mobile electrons in metals are often described as 'a sea of electrons'.
e: True. These mobile electrons in metals are often described as 'a sea of electrons'. Those mobile electrons let metals conduct heat and electricity and explain metallic bonding.

q: The 'sea of electrons' prevents metals from conducting electricity.
e: False. That mobile sea is exactly why metals conduct. The electrons can drift through the lattice when a voltage is applied.

q: The positively charged metallic nuclei are surrounded by fixed, stationary electrons.
e: False. The valence electrons in a metal are mobile, not fixed. That movement is the metallic bond and the reason for conductivity.

q: Metals are held together by a strong electrostatic attraction that results in low volatility of the metals.
e: True. Metals are held together by a strong electrostatic attraction that results in low volatility of the metals. Strong metallic bonding holds atoms in the lattice, so few metals evaporate easily.

q: The strength of metallic bonding increases with the decreasing positive charge on the ions in the metal lattice.
e: False. A larger positive charge on the metal ions pulls the electron sea more strongly. Strength rises with charge, not with decreasing charge.

q: The strength of metallic bonding increases with the decreasing size of metal ions in the lattice.
e: True. The strength of metallic bonding increases with the decreasing size of metal ions in the lattice. A smaller, more highly charged ion pulls the electron sea more tightly.

q: The strength of metallic bonding increases with the increasing number of mobile electrons per atom.
e: True. The strength of metallic bonding increases with the increasing number of mobile electrons per atom. More delocalised electrons mean a stronger metallic bond.

q: The strength of a metallic bond is generally higher than that of an ionic bond.
e: False. Ionic bonds are generally stronger than metallic bonds. That is why many ionic compounds melt higher than the parent metals.

q: Consequently, the melting points of some metals become lower compared with ionic compounds.
e: True. Consequently, the melting points of some metals become lower compared with ionic compounds. Ionic lattices are often held more tightly than metallic ones, so many salts melt higher.
